title: Inner v. Outer Scorecards
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Borrowing Warren Buffett's concept of inner versus outer scorecards, Stuart examines how external-validation-seeking corrodes professional quality and personal flourishing among educators. He applies Buffett's litmus test — would you rather genuinely be great at something but be judged poorly, or genuinely be poor at it but be judged as great — to teaching, parenting, and intellectual life, finding each domain worse when the outer scorecard becomes primary. Stuart catalogues the specific pressures educators face toward external orientation: complex evaluation rubrics, social media, and AI-assisted image management. The article's core argument is not that external measures are morally wrong but that they do not work as organizing principles — obsessing over outcomes and appearances is a spiritual black hole that consumes finite energy without producing the growth it promises. The closing draws on John Wooden's definition of success to establish that outer validation is properly a byproduct of inner-driven excellence, and ends with a practical call to spend less time on eval rubrics and more time on genuine professional development.
points: The outer scorecard measures how others judge us; the inner scorecard measures how we judge ourselves — and the two cannot be simultaneously optimized because finite human energy forces a choice.

An external attitude toward professional identity does not yield optimal human growth — not because it is immoral but because it functionally does not work; obsessing over outcomes is a spiritual black hole.

Teacher evaluation systems structured around observed performances often produce inauthentic teaching rather than genuine improvement, illustrating how outer-scorecard pressure backfires on its own stated goals.

External validation is not wrong or bad, but it becomes corrosive when made ultimate — the people who do the most important work tend to experience it as a side effect of inner-driven excellence, not as the goal.

John Wooden's definition of success — 'knowing you did your best to become the best that you are capable of becoming' — is the inner scorecard in practice, and correlates with the most enduring professional records.
quotes: The big question about how people behave is whether they've got an Inner Scorecard or an Outer Scorecard. It helps if you can be satisfied with an Inner Scorecard. I always pose it this way. I say: 'Lookit. Would you rather be the world's greatest lover, but have everyone think you're the world's worst lover? Or would you rather be the world's worst lover but have everyone think you're the world's greatest lover?'

It's easy to trick ourselves into thinking our external circumstances are the cause of our difficulties and our internal circumstances are beside the point. In reality, it's often the opposite — externals act as magnifiers of what's going on inside.

In our times of complex teacher eval systems, vapid social media hype, and AI-infused fakery, you and I are almost commanded to define ourselves by external measures. It's easier than ever to fool myself (and others) into thinking I'm better at things than I actually am.

an external attitude — Buffet's Outer Scorecard — doesn't yield optimal human growth. It's not that it's naughty but rather that it doesn't work. Obsessing over outcomes doesn't work. Worrying about how we appear to others is a spiritual black hole, ravenous and dense.

The teacher driven simply to get Highly Effective on the eval is unlikely to flourish as much long-term as the teacher pursuing "the full use of their powers along the lines of excellence." We got into this work because it's sacred and precious — not for some eval number.
You can obsess about being a great teacher or about looking like one — you can't obsess about both.

external validation is a cruel and unrelenting taskmaster. Make it ultimate, and it'll ultimately eat you up. It's a wretched Top Priority and a greedy little god. The more I live and observe, the more it seems like the people who live the best lives and do the most important work are those for whom external validation is a side effect of an internal quest for excellence.
